summary: MARS-X is an interactive Mars exploration and mission-planning workstation built on real NASA and USGS planetary datasets. Featuring a 3D CesiumJS globe, it provides terrain analysis, orbital imagery overlays, and rover traverse tracking. The platform computes energy-efficient, hazard-aware A* traverse routes across real MOLA and CTX elevation data for rovers and EVA astronauts. It also integrates Curiosity (REMS) and Perseverance (MEDA) atmospheric observations, prioritizes high-value geological science targets, runs mission digital-twin simulations, and includes an intelligent AI assistant to streamline planetary surface operations.
details:
What it does & How it works:

MARS-X is an interactive Mars exploration and mission-planning workstation. Running on a 3D CesiumJS globe configured for the IAU 2000 Mars sphere, it streams 17 NASA Mars Trek orbital layers, rover paths, and live weather. The FastAPI backend streams NASA MOLA and USGS Jezero CTX elevation data via HTTP Range requests. A custom 8-connected A* graph search evaluates 3D topography, slopes, roughness, and directional traction energy to compute optimal routes (Safest, Shortest, Balanced) with an independent return route and battery feasibility checks. An integrated AI assistant (MARS AI) executes 12 specialized mission tools.

Benefits & Intended Impact:

Unlike static map viewers, MARS-X offers real-time, physics-based surface route calculations, evaluating vehicle energy budgets and astronaut EVA limits in seconds. It bridges the gap between raw NASA telemetry and operational planning for future crewed and robotic Martian exploration.

Tools & Technologies:

- Frontend: Next.js 16, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, CesiumJS (Mars spheroids).

- Backend: Python (FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, Pillow, SQLAlchemy).

- Data & APIs: NASA MGS MOLA altimetry, USGS CTX DTM, Mars Trek WMTS, and REMS/MEDA weather feeds.

- AI & Hosting: Claude API tool loop, Docker, Vercel, and Render.

Creativity & Factors Considered:

We used true Martian physics (3.72 m/s² gravity, spherical geodesy, and directional slope resistance). The system tracks scientific provenance by distinguishing between direct laser-shot measurements and interpolated data, ensuring missions never exceed energy or life-support safety margins.
